papers_read.title_as_printed: Signal and Texture Features from T2 Maps for the Prediction of Mild Cognitive Impairment to Alzheimer's Disease Progression (Trejo-Castro et al., Healthcare 2021, 9, 941)
Predicting conversion in cognitively normal and mild cognitive impairment individuals with machine learning: Is the CSF status still relevant? (Russo et al., Alzheimer's Dement. 2025;21:e14398)

what_each_reports.P-183: N = 40 ADNI MCI aged 70-80 (18 progressed to AD by 2 years, 22 stable at least 5 years); baseline T2-map signal/texture features plus 8 neuropsychological scores; 100 random 80/20 splits. Best accuracy 0.775 (BSWiMS and RF; 95% CI 0.615-0.892); neuropsychology-only best LASSO accuracy 0.675 / ROC AUC 0.727.
what_each_reports.P-308: N = 648 ADNI participants who were CN or MCI at baseline (90 converters: CN->MCI or MCI->AD within 3 years); predictors are standard clinical data (demographics, drug classes, neuropsychology) plus CSF t-tau/Abeta1-42 categorisation, no MRI; after random undersampling of non-converters the gradient-boosting model was applied to 409 participants (22% converters): test accuracy 84%, sensitivity 43%, specificity 96%; 88% in the AD-like-CSF sub-cohort and 86% in the normal-CSF sub-cohort.

quantity_a: Accuracy of classifying MCI progressing to AD within 2 years vs MCI stable at least 5 years, from T2-map radiomics plus neuropsychology, ADNI MCI only, N = 40, repeated internal holdout.
quantity_b: Accuracy of classifying 3-year conversion to the next cognitive level (CN->MCI or MCI->AD) in a pooled CN + MCI sample, from standard clinical data and CSF biomarkers (no imaging), after undersampling, internal train/test split.
incompatible_if_same: No. Even taking the corrected P-183 accuracy (0.775) against 0.84, P-183's own 95% interval (0.615-0.892) contains 0.84, so the two accuracies would not be incompatible even on one quantity. Neither paper claims an ordering that the other refutes.

gates.task: mismatch: P-183 is MCI->AD (T2) with 2-year progressers vs 5-year stables; P-308's endpoint pools CN->MCI and MCI->AD conversion within 3 years, so its positive class is not the T2 label.
gates.modality_family: mismatch: P-183 is T2-map MRI plus neuropsychology; P-308 is clinical/neuropsychological data plus CSF biomarkers with no MRI input. The record's 'Neuroimaging' label is wrong for P-308.

endpoint_and_metric: incompatible: different endpoint (MCI->AD 2-year vs any-level conversion within 3 years in CN + MCI), different horizon, different population behind the label; claim_a's 72.7 is an ROC AUC, not an accuracy, so even the recorded metric types did not match.
performance_validity: flag does not apply: neither result is >= 0.97 (P-308's training accuracies of 91-95% are not the reported test figure and are not the contested quantity).
independence: Both draw on ADNI; overlapping MCI participants are possible. Distinct author groups.
grounds: P-308's outcome pools CN->MCI and MCI->AD conversion in a CN + MCI sample, while P-183's outcome is MCI->AD alone, so the populations behind the conversion label differ.
P-308's predictors are clinical data and CSF biomarkers with no MRI, while P-183's are T2-map radiomics plus neuropsychology; the predictor set and modality family differ, and no waiver is on record.
The horizons differ: 2-year progression vs a 5-year-stable comparator in P-183, and a 3-year window in P-308.
Claim_a misstates P-183 (0.727 is a neuropsychology-only AUC). Its corrected best accuracy (0.775, CI 0.615-0.892) would not exclude 0.84 anyway.

evidence_quotes.quote: The participants were labeled as “converters” depending on whether their cognitive status progressed within 3 years, that is, (1) from CN to MCI; (2) from MCI to AD.
ML was applied to predict the 3-year conversion with standard clinical data (SCD), assess the model’s accuracy, and identify the role of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers in this approach.

After undersampling, the model was applied to 409 participants (22% converters). With the optimal cut-off, the model’s accuracy was 91% in the training set and 84% in the test set. The algorithm showed high specificity (96%) but low sensitivity (43%).

the 18 subjects who had their first AD diagnosis 2 years after their baseline visit were regarded as progressers (MCIp), while the 22 subjects who never had an AD diagnosis and participated in the study for at least 5 years were labeled as stable (MCIs).
The machine learning technique with the best results was LASSO, with an accuracy of 0.675 and an ROC AUC of 0.727.

record_defects: claim_a 'P-183: Acc 72.7 on T2' is wrong: 0.727 is the ROC AUC of the neuropsychology-only LASSO model; P-183's best accuracy is 0.775.
claim_b 'P-308: Acc 84 on T2' mislabels the task: P-308's 84% is for 3-year conversion in pooled CN + MCI (CN->MCI or MCI->AD), not MCI->AD alone.
modality_family 'Neuroimaging' is wrong for P-308, which uses no imaging (clinical data plus CSF). The registry Modality 'MRI/PET' for P-308 is also wrong.
validation_comparable 'Yes' hides that P-308 undersampled non-converters before the train/test evaluation and reports sensitivity of only 43%.
what_would_change_the_verdict: An MCI-only, MCI->AD result from P-308 with a reported interval excluding P-183's 0.775, on a comparable predictor set. P-308 reports no such MCI-only accuracy, and the predictor sets would still differ.
